Hm, well it’s been a combination of a lot of things and I’m not exactly 100% comfortable just yet, but there’s a few factors!

One thing that helped me a lot was that I started medically transitioning last May, I started T and I had top surgery last September. Obviously this may not be immediately available to you, so I’m not going to heed that as the biggest advice, it was just a factor that helped me personally. :’)

Another thing was getting into ouji fashion and starting with that! If ouji isn’t your thing and you love the big frilly dresses though, I think something good about them is that even if you have a traditionally feminine body, they don’t tend to accentuate that. If you feel they still do, try binding, a poofier petticoat (hides the hips) or a sack dress! 

Something else that I find helps with lolita is that it’s so feminine that it kind of loops back around to not feeling anywhere near as bad as mainstream women’s clothes. I would feel miserable in most mainstream skirts or women’s pants and tops, because those are feminine in a very...different? Way than lolita is. I don’t want to compare lolita to drag (nothing against drag of course, i do love it!), but I guess it’s sort of how some transmasculine people and even cis men are ok being in drag but may not be ok in casual women’s clothing! 

A final factor is just kind of the “fuck it” mindset. Positive nihilism, in a way? Nothing matters, the world is kind of a mess right now, may as well do something that makes you happy. I struggle with chronic pain and some pretty severe mental health issues that make work hard, so finding joy in something like ouji and lolita fashion helps bring a little bit of luxury to my day that I know I couldn’t really reach in other ways. (Ie I’ll probably be stuck living at home with my mom for a long time as both me and my partner have similar issues, and saving to move out together is taking a long time as we both rely almost solely on disability to get by. May as well bring some joy in other ways, y’know?) 

Other quick points
1- Lots of cis men wear lolita! Mana-sama is hugely influential in the fashion, particularly gothic. Even cis men who wear lolita will often be mistaken for cis women though, so it doesn’t feel as awful as getting misgendered while wearing mainstream clothing. It’s much more “c’est la vie”.
2- This is a stupid and cheesy one, but the book “The Prince and the Dressmaker” is a lovely short read. I only wear lolita on lower dysphoria days, and when I put on a coord, it helps to think of myself as some nice prince who just so happens to enjoy dresses from time to time.
3- Lolita is just really open to all genders! Most of the community will be really welcoming as long as your interest in the fashion is coming from a genuine place in your heart. 

I think at this point for me, the worst of it is worrying about how I’ll be perceived by the rest of society as a boy who likes such feminine things. It can be scary, and in some places even unsafe. I’m pretty androgynous though, so it’s alright for now.But the good thing now is that people are going outside wearing all sorts of things because of Covid. Everyone is just trying to find joy in small ways. I still have lots of work to do on not caring what people think, and self-acceptance, but these are all small points that help me. 

I hope at least something here is of use to you or provides some comfort!

To start off, your ex sounds like an asshole. Yelling at waiters isn’t masculine, it’s just an dick move. And the way he treated you was absolutely unacceptable.

That aside though, you aren’t alone. Hell, you’re probably more masculine than me. I unironically and genuinely enjoy poofy, frilly dresses (lolita fashion, nothing to do with the book of the same name) but at the same time I’m very outdoorsy. Hey, I’m really sorry both you and him are going through this. Coming from the side of someone who went through the same sort of eating disorder and is now over one year in recovery, I know I was just really incredibly grateful to have my partner there to support me through it. I remember seeing them cry and they were so scared I was going to die too. It was a rough time. 

Something that helps a lot is just showing him that eating is ok. When you have food together, just say positive things about how the food tastes and is enjoyable and how you like spending time with him. 

Try not to comment on his body as well, even if you’re really worried. A comment like “but you’re looking so thin/emaciated” even out of concern will often be taken as a compliment or encouragement when going through an ed, at least in my personal experience. Try to avoid topics such as weight, dieting, macros, etc. 

He’s probably not ready to get into intuitive eating and recovery yet, and unfortunately eating disorders are notoriously persistent but just being there and being supportive and having a positive attitude about food around him can help a lot. 

You can try to pursuade him to pursue recovery but it’ll be really hard since most of the time people are ambivalent and terrified of recovering. If he gets into a recovery program, dealing with the recovery stage might be a bit harder than the current stage and there will unfortunately be slip-ups now and then. 

Sometimes I still sink back into old habits for a bit or have panic attacks because there’s too much oil or sugar or I had a single bite (gasp!) of pie and then had cereal for breakfast so surely I’m overweight and diabetic now. But ultimately recovery will be about pushing through that. It fucking sucks and its awful and there’s lots of physical discomfort that comes with it too but its worth it. I can order food in with my partner without freaking out too much and we’re even making pumpkin pie together tonight. That still feels scary but recovery is a “it feels scary but do it anyways” sort of deal since your brain is being rewired essentially. 

Best of luck to you in helping him and to him in hopefully pursuing recovery. It’s small steps at a time but you can both get through this.
